title: A verse alone (Genesis 1:1)
hookLine: read Bereshit bara Elohim in Hebrew, by yourself

cards: A single line of Hebrew, black letters, no English underneath. For a long stretch now, this path has handed you pieces: the shapes of letters, their sounds, the roots hiding inside words.
Somebody else always did the reading. Today the roles switch. Here is the line the Torah scroll begins with: Bereshit bara Elohim et hashamayim ve'et ha'aretz.
In the King James words, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Today you take it apart yourself, word by word, and put it back together.

teach.b: Go slowly. First, bereshit. The opening letter, bet, is a little word glued on the front: in.
Then reshit, beginning. Some readers hear rosh inside it, the word for head, as in Rosh Hashanah, the head of the year. Second, bara, created.
Its letters are bet, resh, alef. Now look back at bereshit: bet, resh, alef are its first three letters too. The verb is hiding inside the first word before you even reach it.
Elohim follows: God. Third, a word English can't translate at all: et. It's spelled alef, tav, the first letter of the alphabet and the last.

In Hebrew grammar it simply points ahead to the thing being acted on. But some readers have seen more in it: the whole alphabet, beginning to end, standing at the start of the world. Fourth, the pair at the end.
Hashamayim, the heavens; ha is the. Ve'et ha'aretz, and the earth; ve is and, and there's et again, pointing at the earth too. Everything above, everything below.
Bereshit bara Elohim et hashamayim ve'et ha'aretz.
You've just read the Torah's opening line in the language it was written in, one word at a time.
That's a verse alone: a line short enough to hold in one breath.

how: Genesis 1:1 opens the Torah and is read aloud in synagogue each year when the reading cycle begins again after Simchat Torah; some Jewish learners practice reading Hebrew on verses like this one, word by word.

o: a single line copied out by hand for study
a verse recited alone, without a congregation
reading one verse, Genesis 1:1, in Hebrew by yourself

games.q: a verse alone — tap the pairs.

s: bara's letters are the first three letters of bereshit
bet, resh, alef: the verb hides inside the first word.
et is alef and tav. it points to the thing acted on, and English has no word for it. ve means and.
some readers hear rosh, head, inside bereshit
reshit, beginning, sounds like rosh, as in Rosh Hashanah.

games.q: you're reading Genesis 1:1 in Hebrew and reach et, alef and tav, a word English skips. what do some readers see in it?
o: a scribe's mistake to be ignored.
the whole alphabet, first letter to last.
games.why: grammar says et points to the object, but some readers see the whole alef-bet, alef to tav, standing at the start of the world.

practice: Say the verse one word per breath, bereshit, then bara, Elohim, et, hashamayim, ve'et ha'aretz, without rushing to the meaning; then say the whole verse once at your own pace, and if you stumble, start again, since there's no audience.
If you pray, you can let the verse itself be your words, the way it opens the Torah each year. Otherwise, let the last two words stay with you: the heavens, and the earth you're sitting on.

wordCard.voice: A verse alone. Genesis one, verse one, read by yourself in Hebrew: bereshit bara Elohim et hashamayim ve'et ha'aretz. In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: in the beginning God created; the opening words of Genesis 1:1.

carryVoice: Your line: bereshit bara. In the beginning, created: the Torah's first two words, read by you. Tomorrow, the close of the whole year.
